short: The traditional founder of Japan's imperial line, and a figure with no historical record behind him.
full:
The Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720 describe Jimmu as a descendant of the sun goddess Amaterasu who marched east from Kyushu, subdued the Yamato plain and took the throne. The eighth-century compilers dated that accession to a year corresponding to 660 BCE and gave him a reign of seventy-six years, ending in 585 BCE. Both dates are traditional rather than recorded. The 660 figure appears to have been produced by counting back from the compilers' own century in cycles borrowed from Chinese calendrical numerology to reach an auspicious year.

No evidence exists for Jimmu or for the eight sovereigns said to have followed him, and historians treat the whole early sequence as a later construction giving the Yamato rulers a divine pedigree. The story nonetheless had political force. Meiji-era Japan fixed 11 February as National Foundation Day on the strength of it, and the claim of an unbroken line descending from Jimmu became a pillar of State Shinto until Emperor Shōwa's 1946 rescript disowned it.
